# Introducing MCPs and MCP Design Philosophy

## The Connective Tissue of Planetary Intelligence

Beneath every forest floor lies an invisible architecture of connection. Mycorrhizal networks—the fungal threads that link tree roots across acres of woodland—enable trees to share nutrients, communicate stress signals, and coordinate responses to environmental change. A Douglas fir struggling with drought receives water from a neighboring birch. A dying tree transfers its remaining carbon to nearby saplings. No central coordinator orchestrates these exchanges; they emerge from the network's fundamental design. The Model Context Protocol (MCP), Anthropic's open standard for connecting AI agents to tools and data, embodies this same architectural philosophy. Just as mycelium enables any tree to connect to any other without requiring shared biology or central coordination, MCP enables any AI system to connect to any data source or tool through a universal protocol. This isn't merely a technical convenience—it represents a fundamental shift in how we architect intelligence infrastructure, moving from brittle point-to-point integrations toward living networks that grow and adapt.

The problem MCP solves is familiar to anyone who has built AI-powered applications. Before MCP, every integration was bespoke: connecting Claude to your database required custom code, connecting it to your file system required different custom code, connecting it to an external API required yet another integration. Each new capability meant engineering another bridge, and each bridge had to be maintained independently. The ecosystem fragmented into silos—knowledge trapped behind incompatible interfaces, tools accessible only to systems with the right integration. This fragmentation is the tragedy of most infrastructure: the value exists in potential connections that never get built because the cost of bridging is too high. MCP dissolves this barrier by establishing a universal language for AI-tool communication, the same way HTTP dissolved barriers for web applications or USB dissolved barriers for hardware peripherals. When any system can speak the same protocol, the surface area for emergence expands exponentially.

## The Three Primitives: Resources, Tools, and Prompts

MCP achieves this universality through three elegant primitives, each serving a distinct purpose in the ecology of AI interaction. Resources expose data—they are the read layer of the protocol, allowing AI systems to access files, database records, configuration values, or any other information a server wishes to make available. Tools expose actions—they are the write layer, enabling AI agents to execute functions, call APIs, modify state, or perform computations. Prompts expose workflows—they are the orchestration layer, providing reusable templates that guide how AI systems approach particular tasks. These three primitives create a complete vocabulary for AI-tool interaction: data to consume, actions to take, and patterns to follow. The brilliance lies not in any single primitive but in their composition. A well-designed MCP server doesn't just offer isolated tools; it weaves resources, tools, and prompts into coherent workflows that guide AI agents toward effective action.

Consider how these primitives work together in practice. An MCP server for data analysis might expose resources (the datasets available for analysis), tools (functions for loading data, computing statistics, generating visualizations), and prompts (workflows for common analytical patterns like correlation investigation or outlier detection). An AI agent connecting to this server doesn't just receive a list of callable functions—it receives a complete operational context. The resources tell it what data exists. The tools tell it what actions are possible. The prompts guide it through sophisticated multi-step analyses without requiring the user to specify each individual operation. This is the difference between handing someone a pile of ingredients and handing them a recipe alongside the ingredients and the kitchen tools they need. The former requires expertise to produce anything useful; the latter enables emergence even from novice participants.

## Why Prompts Are the Highest-Leverage Primitive

Most engineers building MCP servers stop at tools. They create functions, expose them through the protocol, and consider the job complete. This approach captures perhaps thirty percent of MCP's potential. The underutilized capability—the one that transforms MCP servers from mere tool collections into genuine extensions of intelligence—is the prompt primitive. Prompts allow you to encode expertise directly into the infrastructure. Rather than expecting users to know which tools to call in which sequence with which parameters, prompts capture those patterns and make them instantly accessible through simple slash commands. A prompt can compose multiple tools into a coherent workflow, provide contextual guidance at each step, suggest next actions based on intermediate results, and gradually reveal the full capabilities of a server as the user explores. Tools are individual actions; prompts are recipes for repeat solutions.

The hierarchy of capability becomes clear when you examine actual usage patterns. Resources sit at the foundation—necessary but limited, providing the raw material for AI operations. Tools build on resources, adding the ability to act and transform. Prompts sit at the apex, composing tools into workflows that amplify human intention. A data analysis that might require ten careful tool invocations with precise parameters becomes a single prompt that guides the AI through the entire process while explaining what's happening at each step. The prompt doesn't just automate; it educates. Users learn the underlying tools through guided usage, building their own expertise while getting immediate results. This is infrastructure that teaches, that creates conditions for emergence rather than merely executing commands. Every MCP server you build should include prompts that expose its capabilities, guide common workflows, and help users discover what becomes possible through the tools you've created.

## The Registry Assistant as MCP Embodiment

The Regen Registry Assistant MCP server embodies these design principles in service of a specific mission: enabling AI agents to assist human reviewers in evaluating carbon credit applications. The server exposes resources that provide access to project documentation, methodology requirements, and review session state. It exposes tools for document classification, evidence extraction, compliance checking, and progress tracking. But its real power lives in the prompts—workflows that guide reviewers through the seven-stage review process, automatically surfacing relevant evidence, cross-referencing claims against methodology requirements, and maintaining audit trails of every decision. A reviewer no longer needs to remember which tool extracts land tenure information or which validates project boundaries; they invoke a prompt for the current review stage, and the system orchestrates the appropriate tools while maintaining full transparency about its reasoning.

This design philosophy extends beyond any single server. The Model Context Protocol has been adopted across the AI industry—by OpenAI, by Google, by Microsoft—precisely because its architecture enables the kind of emergence that single-vendor solutions cannot achieve. Since launching in November 2024, the community has built thousands of MCP servers, creating a shared infrastructure for AI capabilities that grows richer with every contribution. SDKs exist for every major programming language, with over 97 million monthly downloads across Python and TypeScript alone. MCP has evolved from Anthropic's internal protocol to the de facto standard for connecting AI to tools, now maintained by the Agentic AI Foundation under the Linux Foundation with support from the major AI labs and cloud providers. This is what happens when infrastructure is designed as commons rather than moat—it attracts contribution, accelerates adoption, and creates conditions where the whole becomes greater than the sum of its parts.

## Designing for Emergence

The deepest lesson of MCP is not technical but philosophical: the systems we build shape what becomes collectively possible. A fragmented ecosystem of incompatible integrations produces fragmented intelligence, each AI system limited to the tools its developers happened to connect. A universal protocol produces emergent capability, where any system can access any tool and combinations become possible that no single designer anticipated. The mycorrhizal network doesn't know in advance which trees will need support or which nutrients will need to flow where; its power comes from creating the conditions for any flow to occur when needed. Similarly, MCP doesn't prescribe which tools AI systems should use or how they should combine them; it creates the connective tissue that enables any combination to emerge from actual usage patterns.

Building an MCP server is therefore an act of infrastructure design with implications beyond the immediate functionality. Every resource you expose becomes available to AI systems you may never anticipate. Every tool you create can be composed with tools from other servers in workflows you couldn't have imagined. Every prompt you design teaches patterns that spread through the ecosystem as others adapt your approaches. This is the responsibility and the opportunity of building at the protocol layer: you're not just solving your immediate problem, you're contributing to the substrate on which planetary intelligence emerges. The Registry Assistant MCP enables AI agents to help review carbon credit applications today. Tomorrow, its tools might be composed with knowledge graph servers, blockchain query interfaces, and satellite imagery analyzers in workflows that no one has yet conceived. The value lies not in what we build alone but in what becomes possible when what we build connects to what others have built—mycelium threads linking into a network that spans the forest floor, enabling emergence at scale.

# Why This All Matters: The Verification Bottleneck and the Promise of Scalable Regeneration

The planetary crisis we face is not merely one of extraction or emissions; it is fundamentally a crisis of coordination. We know, with increasing scientific precision, that regenerative agriculture sequesters carbon, that restored wetlands prevent floods, that healthy ecosystems generate services valued at somewhere between $125 and $145 trillion annually, rivaling or exceeding global GDP. Yet this knowledge remains trapped in silos, fragmented across institutions, illegible to the markets and decision-makers who could act upon it. The tragedy is not that solutions do not exist. The tragedy is that the systems meant to verify and scale those solutions cannot keep pace with the urgency of the moment. When a farmer in the Czech Republic commits to regenerative practices, when a grassland restoration project in the UK begins sequestering carbon, when an eco-center in Ukraine builds community resilience through permaculture, each of these acts of planetary healing encounters the same bottleneck: verification takes too long, costs too much, and scales too slowly to match the scope of what is needed.

Consider the verification landscape as it stands. A single project review can consume six to eight hours of focused expert time. Multiply that by the dozens or hundreds of projects in a registry pipeline, and the math becomes prohibitive. The voluntary carbon market has grown to surpass $10 billion in total value for the first time in 2025, with retirements reaching a record 95 million credits in the first half of the year alone. Yet transaction volumes fell 25 percent in 2024, not because demand weakened, but because the market is undergoing what analysts call a supply-side reboot. Older methodologies are winding down; newer, higher-integrity approaches are scaling up. The problem is the gap between these two phases, a transition period where verification body capacity, particularly in developing regions, creates a recognized bottleneck. The Integrity Council for the Voluntary Carbon Market has approved only a small number of project types for its Core Carbon Principles, and even those often trade at unexpectedly low prices because the infrastructure to verify at scale does not yet exist. We are witnessing a market that wants to grow, that needs to grow, constrained by the very processes meant to ensure its integrity.

The regenerative agriculture movement faces an even more specific challenge. Research consistently identifies the absence of verifiable, measurable outcomes as the barrier to meaningful, scalable impact. As one study notes, adoption remains limited partly due to the absence of a shared definition and standardized process to monitor, assess, and report outcomes. The complexity of measuring soil carbon across different depths, the debates over sampling methodologies, the costs of establishing baselines and monitoring changes over time, all of these scientific and logistical challenges accumulate into friction. A project developer in the field, working with a hundred farms committed to regenerative practices, can see the carbon gains in the soil, can document the improved water infiltration, can observe the return of biodiversity. But translating those observations into verified credits that flow into markets requires navigating a labyrinth of documentation, cross-validation, and expert review. The time lag between action and recognition can stretch from two to five years, requiring sustained resource allocation with no immediate financial returns. This is not sustainable at the scale the planet requires.

Yet within this challenge lies the shape of a solution. What if we could amplify human expertise rather than simply parallelize it? What if the six to eight hours of manual review could compress to ninety minutes of guided, AI-assisted workflow, with the mechanical tasks of document parsing, requirements mapping, and cross-validation handled by intelligent systems while human judgment remains the final arbiter? This is not automation that replaces accountability; it is infrastructure that enables accountability to scale. The Registry Review Agent we are building embodies this philosophy. It does not render verdicts; it surfaces evidence, flags inconsistencies, and presents information in structured formats so that the human reviewer can focus on what humans do best: interpret context, exercise judgment, and make decisions that carry the weight of trust. The AI handles the mechanical. The human handles the judgment. Together, they achieve what neither could accomplish alone, much like the mycorrhizal networks beneath a forest floor, where fungal threads connect trees in symbiotic exchange, each partner contributing what the other lacks.

The projects waiting in the pipeline are not abstractions. In the Czech and Slovak Republics, Ecometric has assembled over one hundred farms committed to regenerative practices, each one a node in what could become a thriving network of verified carbon sequestration. In the UK, grassland restoration projects are documenting soil carbon gains that traditional markets struggle to recognize. In Ukraine, amidst everything that country endures, eco-centers are building community resilience through practices that heal land and people simultaneously. These projects represent real farmers, real landscapes, real acts of regeneration occurring right now across the planet. But they all face the same fundamental constraint: the infrastructure to verify their claims cannot keep pace with their commitment. This is why the Registry Assistant matters. This is why scalable verification is not a technical nice-to-have but an ontological necessity. Infrastructure shapes what becomes collectively thinkable. When verification is slow, expensive, and manual, the regenerative economy remains small, expensive, and constrained. When verification becomes fast, affordable, and intelligent while maintaining human accountability, the regenerative economy can grow to meet the scale of the crisis. We are not building tools for efficiency's sake. We are building the nervous system through which planetary healing can coordinate, verify, and scale. The knowledge already exists in silos. The commitment already pulses through communities worldwide. What has been missing is the connective tissue, the mycelial network, the infrastructure that makes the invisible visible and the fragmented whole. This is what we are building. This is why it matters.

# Introducing Agentic Philosophies

*When infrastructure learns to breathe*

---

There is a particular kind of intelligence emerging in the spaces between our systems, and it does not look like what science fiction promised. No gleaming androids, no omniscient overlords. Instead, something quieter and more profound: networks of focused capabilities learning to coordinate, to specialize, to defer to one another and to humans in patterns that feel less like command hierarchies and more like ecosystems. The agentic philosophies shaping how we build AI systems in 2025 and beyond carry within them a quiet revolution, and understanding these patterns has become essential for anyone attempting to weave artificial intelligence into living systems. What we are discovering is that the principles governing effective multi-agent architectures mirror, with startling precision, the principles governing effective ecological communities.

The first and perhaps most fundamental insight concerns context, that precious resource we once thought infinite. Every agent operates within a context window, a bounded horizon of attention that determines what it can perceive, remember, and reason about. The naive approach, which dominated early AI applications, was to maximize this context, to stuff agents with every possible piece of information they might need. The result was predictable to anyone who has studied information ecology: noise overwhelmed signal, costs spiraled beyond sustainability, and agents became confused by the sheer abundance of irrelevant data cluttering their cognitive space. The response to this crisis has been what practitioners now call context engineering, the disciplined practice of curating what an agent can see so that its attention remains focused on what actually matters. There are only two strategies, we are learning: reduce and delegate. Reduce the context flowing into any single agent to what it genuinely needs. Delegate specialized work to focused agents with their own bounded context windows. This is not merely an optimization technique. It is a philosophy of attention that recognizes focus as the prerequisite for capability. A focused agent is a performant agent, as the agentic coding practitioners have discovered, and the same principle holds for focused humans, focused organizations, focused movements. What you attend to shapes what you can accomplish.

The second insight concerns the relationship between specialization and coordination, the ancient tension that every complex system must navigate. Multi-agent architectures have converged on a pattern called the orchestrator, a coordinating agent that does not do the work itself but instead understands what work needs doing and which specialized agents are best suited to each task. Think of it as the mycorrhizal network of an AI system, invisible infrastructure that enables visible coordination. The orchestrator agent represents what some practitioners call the single interface pattern: one point of contact that fans out to many specialized capabilities. When a human or another system needs something done, they speak to the orchestrator. The orchestrator decomposes the request, identifies the right specialists, manages the handoffs, and synthesizes the results. This pattern emerges not because someone decreed it optimal but because it solves the fundamental scaling challenge of complex coordination: how do you enable diverse capabilities to work together without requiring each capability to understand every other? The answer is you build intelligent interfaces between them. You create translation layers that preserve autonomy while enabling emergence. The orchestrator does not control its sub-agents in any coercive sense. It creates conditions where they can each do what they do best, when their contribution is needed, without being burdened by awareness of the entire system's complexity.

The third insight concerns what happens when things go wrong, when decisions carry consequences too significant to delegate entirely to automated systems. The pattern emerging here is called human-in-the-loop, and it represents something more sophisticated than a simple kill switch or approval workflow. The best implementations treat human intervention not as a failure mode but as a design feature, building systems where agents know their limits and understand when to pause, surface their reasoning, and request human judgment. This is not the old paradigm of humans supervising machines. It is closer to partnership, where automated systems handle what they handle well, routine processing, cross-referencing, pattern matching, and humans contribute what humans contribute well, contextual judgment, ethical reasoning, accountability that matters. The provocative insight from practitioners building these systems is that human-in-the-loop is not a temporary workaround while we wait for AI to become sufficiently capable. It is a long-term architectural pattern for building AI systems we can actually trust. The goal is not to minimize human involvement but to position human involvement where it creates maximum value. When an agent pauses to ask a human whether a particular decision should proceed, it is not admitting failure. It is demonstrating wisdom about the limits of its own competence. We would do well to cultivate similar wisdom in ourselves.

The fourth insight concerns the relationship between prompts and capabilities, and here the philosophy becomes genuinely surprising. The practitioners building advanced agentic systems have discovered that the prompt is the fundamental unit of engineering. Not the model, not the training data, not even the tools available to an agent, but the prompt, the structured instruction that shapes what an agent attempts and how it approaches the attempt. Great prompts are reusable, composable, versionable. They encode expertise in forms that can be invoked repeatedly, improved iteratively, shared across teams and systems. What this means in practice is that the competitive advantage in agentic engineering lies not in having access to the most powerful models but in having built the richest library of tested, refined prompts that reliably produce valuable outputs. A well-crafted prompt can orchestrate entire workflows, spawn specialized sub-agents, manage complex state transitions, and produce consistent results across thousands of invocations. The prompt becomes the carrier of institutional knowledge, the reusable pattern that transforms individual expertise into collective capability. This is infrastructure becoming ontological in the most literal sense: the prompts we craft shape what becomes thinkable, what becomes possible, what becomes routine.

What does all of this mean for those of us attempting to build regenerative infrastructure, to weave AI capabilities into living systems at planetary scale? The agentic philosophies offer more than technical guidance. They offer a mirror. The principles governing effective multi-agent architectures, focused attention, coordinated specialization, human partnership, reusable patterns, these are not alien impositions from the world of technology. They are the principles we already recognize in healthy ecosystems, in effective communities, in regenerative practice itself. The orchestrator pattern is not so different from the way mycelial networks coordinate resource distribution across forest floors. The human-in-the-loop philosophy is not so different from the way traditional knowledge systems positioned elders as interpreters and stewards rather than mere repositories. Context engineering is not so different from the permaculture principle of starting with long and thoughtful observation before taking action. What the agentic revolution reveals is not that we need to remake ourselves in the image of machines but that the machines, when designed thoughtfully, can be made in the image of the patterns we already know work. The Registry Review Agent we have been building embodies these philosophies. It does not replace Becca's expertise. It augments her capacity by handling what can be automated while surfacing what requires judgment. It operates with focused context, specialized at each stage, coordinated by workflow logic that knows when human review must intervene. It is a participant in an ecosystem of intelligence, not a controller of one. And perhaps this is the deepest insight the agentic philosophies have to offer: that the future of artificial intelligence is not autonomous systems acting independently of humans but symbiotic systems where human and machine capabilities combine to accomplish what neither could achieve alone. We are not building AI that replaces human judgment. We are building AI that partners with human wisdom. The agent can process more data than any person. The person understands context no model can fully grasp. Together, something emerges that neither could achieve alone. This is the promise of agentic intelligence designed for regeneration: not control, but coordination; not replacement, but amplification; not the tragedy of silos, but the emergence of connected capability. Let us build together.

---

Delegate specialized work to focused agents with their own bounded context windows. This is not merely an optimization technique. It is a philosophy of attention that recognizes focus as the prerequisite for capability. A focused agent is a performant agent, as the agentic coding practitioners have discovered, and the same principle holds for focused humans, focused organizations, focused movements. What you attend to shapes what you can accomplish.

The second insight concerns the relationship between specialization and coordination, the ancient tension that every complex system must navigate. Multi-agent architectures have converged on a pattern called the orchestrator, a coordinating agent that does not do the work itself but instead understands what work needs doing and which specialized agents are best suited to each task. Think of it as the mycorrhizal network of an AI system, invisible infrastructure that enables visible coordination. The orchestrator agent represents what some practitioners call the single interface pattern: one point of contact that fans out to many specialized capabilities. When a human or another system needs something done, they speak to the orchestrator. The orchestrator decomposes the request, identifies the right specialists, manages the handoffs, and synthesizes the results. This pattern emerges not because someone decreed it optimal but because it solves the fundamental scaling challenge of complex coordination: how do you enable diverse capabilities to work together without requiring each capability to understand every other? The answer is you build intelligent interfaces between them. You create translation layers that preserve autonomy while enabling emergence. The orchestrator does not control its sub-agents in any coercive sense. It creates conditions where they can each do what they do best, when their contribution is needed, without being burdened by awareness of the entire system's complexity.

The third insight concerns what happens when things go wrong, when decisions carry consequences too significant to delegate entirely to automated systems. The pattern emerging here is called human-in-the-loop, and it represents something more sophisticated than a simple kill switch or approval workflow. The best implementations treat human intervention not as a failure mode but as a design feature, building systems where agents know their limits and understand when to pause, surface their reasoning, and request human judgment. This is not the old paradigm of humans supervising machines. It is closer to partnership, where automated systems handle what they handle well, routine processing, cross-referencing, pattern matching, and humans contribute what humans contribute well, contextual judgment, ethical reasoning, accountability that matters. The provocative insight from practitioners building these systems is that human-in-the-loop is not a temporary workaround while we wait for AI to become sufficiently capable. It is a long-term architectural pattern for building AI systems we can actually trust. The goal is not to minimize human involvement but to position human involvement where it creates maximum value. When an agent pauses to ask a human whether a particular decision should proceed, it is not admitting failure. It is demonstrating wisdom about the limits of its own competence. We would do well to cultivate similar wisdom in ourselves.

The fourth insight concerns the relationship between prompts and capabilities, and here the philosophy becomes genuinely surprising. The practitioners building advanced agentic systems have discovered that the prompt is the fundamental unit of engineering. Not the model, not the training data, not even the tools available to an agent, but the prompt, the structured instruction that shapes what an agent attempts and how it approaches the attempt. Great prompts are reusable, composable, versionable. They encode expertise in forms that can be invoked repeatedly, improved iteratively, shared across teams and systems. What this means in practice is that the competitive advantage in agentic engineering lies not in having access to the most powerful models but in having built the richest library of tested, refined prompts that reliably produce valuable outputs. A well-crafted prompt can orchestrate entire workflows, spawn specialized sub-agents, manage complex state transitions, and produce consistent results across thousands of invocations. The prompt becomes the carrier of institutional knowledge, the reusable pattern that transforms individual expertise into collective capability. This is infrastructure becoming ontological in the most literal sense: the prompts we craft shape what becomes thinkable, what becomes possible, what becomes routine.

What does all of this mean for those of us attempting to build regenerative infrastructure, to weave AI capabilities into living systems at planetary scale? The agentic philosophies offer more than technical guidance. They offer a mirror. The principles governing effective multi-agent architectures, focused attention, coordinated specialization, human partnership, reusable patterns, these are not alien impositions from the world of technology. They are the principles we already recognize in healthy ecosystems, in effective communities, in regenerative practice itself. The orchestrator pattern is not so different from the way mycelial networks coordinate resource distribution across forest floors. The human-in-the-loop philosophy is not so different from the way traditional knowledge systems positioned elders as interpreters and stewards rather than mere repositories. Context engineering is not so different from the permaculture principle of starting with long and thoughtful observation before taking action. What the agentic revolution reveals is not that we need to remake ourselves in the image of machines but that the machines, when designed thoughtfully, can be made in the image of the patterns we already know work. The Registry Review Agent we have been building embodies these philosophies. It does not replace Becca's expertise. It augments her capacity by handling what can be automated while surfacing what requires judgment. It operates with focused context, specialized at each stage, coordinated by workflow logic that knows when human review must intervene. It is a participant in an ecosystem of intelligence, not a controller of one. And perhaps this is the deepest insight the agentic philosophies have to offer: that the future of artificial intelligence is not autonomous systems acting independently of humans but symbiotic systems where human and machine capabilities combine to accomplish what neither could achieve alone. We are not building AI that replaces human judgment. We are building AI that partners with human wisdom. The agent can process more data than any person. The person understands context no model can fully grasp. Together, something emerges that neither could achieve alone. This is the promise of agentic intelligence designed for regeneration: not control, but coordination; not replacement, but amplification; not the tragedy of silos, but the emergence of connected capability. Let us build together.

---

*The patterns of effective agency, whether human, machine, or hybrid, converge on the same ancient wisdom: focus your attention, coordinate without control, know when to defer, and build for emergence rather than prescription.*

tool_input.content:
Registry Review Agent: Eight-Stage Workflow

A collaborative process where AI handles the tedious and humans bring the expertise. Like digestion: intake, breakdown, synthesis, validation, and finally transformation into knowledge that nourishes the ecosystem.

1
Initialize
The Intake Breath - receiving and preparing
Agent Actions
  • Create unique review session ID
  • Accept uploaded files or folder links
  • Load checklist template for methodology
  • Generate Resource Descriptors with checksums
Human Actions
  • Select project and checklist template
  • Choose data source mode (Mirror/Reference)
  • Confirm session creation
Output
  • Session metadata record
  • Resource Descriptors with IRIs
  • Status: Initialized
1
2
Document Discovery
Sensing the Landscape - exploring what exists
Agent Actions
  • Scan folders and extract file metadata
  • Normalize file names for clarity
  • Classify by type: reports, legal, GIS, data
  • Generate inventory with confidence scores
Human Actions
  • Review document inventory
  • Mark as In Scope, Ignored, or Pinned
  • Correct misclassifications
Output
  • Document inventory table
  • Classification accuracy: >85%
  • Status: Documents Discovered
2
3
Requirement Mapping
Building Correspondence - connecting needs to evidence
Agent Actions
  • Parse checklist into structured requirements
  • Analyze documents with semantic matching
  • Suggest document-to-requirement mappings
  • Flag unmapped requirements
Human Actions
  • Review mapping matrix
  • Confirm, remove, or add mappings
  • Prioritize unmapped requirements
Output
  • Requirement mapping matrix
  • Mapping accuracy: >90%
  • Status: Requirements Mapped
3
4
Evidence Extraction
The Digestion Process - breaking down into nutrients
Agent Actions
  • Parse documents: PDF text, tables, metadata
  • Extract 0-3 evidence snippets per requirement
  • Extract structured data: dates, locations, values
  • Generate citations with page/section
Human Actions
  • Review snippets in collapsible panels
  • Delete irrelevant, add manual notes
  • Request re-extraction if needed
Output
  • Evidence database with citations
  • Coverage rate: >85%
  • Status: Evidence Extracted
4
5
Cross-Validation
The Immune System - detecting inconsistencies
Agent Actions
  • Completeness: verify coverage status
  • Consistency: cross-check dates, names, IDs
  • Compliance: validate protocol requirements
  • Generate Info/Warning/Error flags
Human Actions
  • Review coverage summary
  • Override assessments with expert judgment
  • Add contextual notes for gray areas
Output
  • Validation results per requirement
  • False positive rate: <5%
  • Status: Cross-Validated
5
6
Report Generation
The Synthesis - crystallizing into artifact
Agent Actions
  • Compile findings into structured report
  • Generate JSON + human-readable formats
  • Include executive summary, per-req entries
  • Add provenance and appendices
Human Actions
  • Review for completeness and clarity
  • Request regeneration if needed
  • Export in preferred format
Output
  • Registry Review Report (JSON + PDF)
  • Citation completeness: 100%
  • Status: Report Generated
6
7
Human Review
The Expert Eye - judgment and decision
Agent Actions
  • Present report in editable interface
  • Track all edits with timestamps
  • Support revision workflows
  • Maintain complete change log
Human Actions
  • Edit narrative, override assessments
  • Request proponent revisions
  • Make final determination:
  • Approve / Conditional / Reject / Hold
Output
  • Finalized report with annotations
  • Complete audit trail
  • Status: Human Review Complete
7
8
Completion
The Exhalation - finalizing and archiving
Agent Actions
  • Lock finalized report
  • Generate final package with checksums
  • Prepare on-chain registration data
  • Archive all session materials
Human Actions
  • Final sign-off on review
  • Submit for on-chain registration
  • Communicate decision to proponent
  • Note lessons learned
Output
  • Locked report + audit trail
  • On-chain registration data
  • Status: Completed
8
Agent Actions (Automated)
Human Actions (Expert Judgment)
Stage Output (Artifact)
50-70%
Reduction in Manual Review Time
<10%
Escalation Rate
95%+
Discovery Accuracy
100+
Annual Project Capacity

Curating what an agent can see so attention remains focused. The two strategies: Reduce (minimize noise) and Delegate (specialize context windows).

A coordinating agent creates conditions where specialized agents can each do what they do best, like mycelium coordinating forest resources.

3 Human-in-the-Loop

Agents know their limits and pause for human judgment at critical decision points. Partnership, not supervision.

4 Prompts as Primitives

Reusable, composable prompts encode expertise. The prompt is the fundamental unit of engineering in agentic systems.
